c.st: Bertrand Russell: In Praise of Idleness (1932)
c.x: I liked a bunch of the essays I read by him, and loved "A History of Western Philosophy". I'm well aware (and felt his writing made it obvious enough) that it is not necessarily a 'accurate' history of philosophy, but it was a great book with a great approach.

In that case, I highly recommend the following:

1) A History of Western Philosophy by Bertrand Russell
2) Philosophy of Language by W. G. Lycan

These two should provide you a general understanding of the field, along with some really interesting articles in language.

Bertrand Russel – A History of Western Philosophy.

Easily my most favorite non-fiction book. Even though there are some flaws in the treatment of some philosophers (and their models) here and there (esp. 19th Century ones –  but it might just be that I'm more familiar with these myself), it's a great read: Well written, thorough, and never shy with his own opinion. The chapter on scholastic philosophy was an eye-opener for me, as was the part about the 11th-Century church reforms.
